rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / DATA AND LOOPS / CHAPTER 6

slides.title: Lists
slides.main: A list is the most used container: one name, many values.

items.title: List
items.sub: One name, many values: Python's core container

items.title: Indexes
items.sub: Count from zero; minus one is the last item

items.title: Add
items.sub: Adds to the end; the list grows on the fly

items.title: Iterate
items.sub: A loop walks the list directly, no counters

body.text: Emails, cart items, friends: reality is made of collections. One variable per value won't scale.

slides.title: Creating a list
slides.main: Good lists are uniform: numbers with numbers, strings with strings.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
empty = []
mixed = [1, "two"]   # better not to do this

cells.sub: A list of three numbers is ready
Empty list: how most programs begin

slides.title: Zero-based indexes
slides.sub: Access by number in square brackets
slides.main: An index is a distance from the start, not a count: the first is zero.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[0])   # 10
print(nums[2])   # 30
print(nums[3])   # error!
ON SCREEN

10
30
IndexError: list index out of range
Three elements: valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2. No third.

slides.title: Negative indexes
slides.sub: Minus one is the last element
slides.main: A negative index always looks at the end, however long the list is.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[-1])   # 30
print(nums[-2])   # 20

cells.title: nums[-1]
cells.sub: The last one, even without knowing the length

cells.title: nums[-2]
cells.sub: Second to last: "two from the end"

slides.title: Changing in place
slides.sub: Assigning by index replaces an element
slides.main: Lists are mutable, unlike strings, which can only be rebuilt.

cells.title: strings ≠ lists
cells.sub: A string can't be changed, a list can: it's alive

slides.title: List length
slides.sub: The len function returns the item count
slides.main: One function counts both string characters and list items.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(len(nums))   # 3
print(len([]))     # 0 — an empty list is still a list

cells.title: len
cells.sub: Known from chapter 2: works on any container

slides.title: Add: append
slides.sub: The append method adds to the end
slides.main: An empty list on line one, a hundred values by line one hundred.

body.text:
nums = []
nums.append(10)
nums.append(20)
print(nums)      # [10, 20]

cells.title: .append(x)
cells.sub: Goes to the end; existing order untouched

slides.title: Looping with for
slides.sub: The loop walks the list directly
slides.main: No counters or hand-made indexes: it reads like English.

body.text:
for x in nums:
    print(x)
ON SCREEN
x becomes each element in turn: Python fetches them in order.

slides.title: Membership: in
slides.sub: Is the item in the list: true or false
slides.main: In chapter 3, in checked a substring; now it checks a list item.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(7 in nums)    # False
print(20 in nums)   # True

cells.title: Check before acting
cells.sub: Is the item in the cart, is the name on the list

slides.title: Removing
slides.sub: remove: by value, pop: from the end
slides.main: remove drops the first match; pop takes one off, like a plate from a stack.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.remove(20)      # crossed out 20
last = nums.pop()    # took 30 off the end
print(nums, last)
ON SCREEN
pop has an index version: it takes the item at that position.

slides.title: Slices
slides.sub: A piece of the list: index one up to three
slides.main: The right bound is excluded: same logic as range in the last chapter.

body.text:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(nums[1:3])   # [20, 30]
print(nums[:2])    # [10, 20]
print(nums[:])     # a copy of the whole list

cells.sub: Empty left: "from the start", empty right: "to the end"
A full slice is a simple way to copy a list

slides.title: Order and summaries
slides.main: max, min and sum are built in, but in exercises we loop by hand.

body.text:
nums = [30, 10, 20]
nums.sort()
print(nums)                    # [10, 20, 30]
print(max(nums), min(nums), sum(nums))
ON SCREEN
sort changes the order for good: no way back.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: A list is good when items are found by number: first, second, last.
